problem: Prior LLM-based robot planning is usually judged with binary success measures, which hide partial progress, and it is unclear how well general-purpose LLMs plan zero-shot from multimodal (visual plus spatial) inputs for autonomous mobile robots.
motivation: Autonomous mobile robots and unmanned systems need adaptive planning without task-specific training. Binary success metrics cannot show partial task completion or orientation errors, so a finer-grained evaluation is needed to tell how far zero-shot LLM planners actually get.
key_idea: A modular architecture feeds visual and spatial inputs to a general-purpose LLM that iteratively plans robot actions in simulation, and a continuous metric combining distance and orientation scores it.
insight: Zero-shot multimodal LLMs show goal-directed spatial planning and partial task completion. Plan quality is inconsistent across models (GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash), which points to a need for task-specific adaptation or fine-tuning. Only the abstract was available, so no specific ablation can be cited.
method: Modular system architecture: a general-purpose LLM is integrated with visual and spatial inputs for adaptive planning.
Iterative planning loop: the LLM's outputs iteratively guide robot behavior in simulation.
Continuous evaluation metric: a single score jointly combines distance and orientation, as a finer-grained alternative to binary success.
Model comparison: three foundation LLMs (GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash) are tested on zero-shot navigation and exploration tasks.

setting.observation: visual inputs plus spatial information (details not given in the abstract)

results: The abstract reports qualitatively that LLMs show encouraging goal-directed spatial planning and partial task completion in zero-shot navigation and exploration. Plan generation is inconsistent across the three models. No numeric results are given.
limitations: Plan generation is inconsistent across models, so zero-shot performance is unreliable.
The evaluation uses small, cheap LLMs in simulation only, with no real-robot validation.
